records.title: Need for a National Programme for the prevention and control of childhood myopia.
details:
Dr. Parmar Jasvantsinh Salamsinh:
I seek to draw attention of the Government to the
rapidly rising burden of myopia among Indian children. Myopia is projected to
affect nearly half the worlds population by 2050, with about ten per cent
developing high myopia. In urban India, prevalence is projected to reach 48 per
cent by 2050, and a marked rise has been recorded even among rural children,
from 4.6 per cent in 1980?2008 to 6.8 per cent in 2009?2019. Correcting
refractive error nationwide is estimated to cost between Rs. 6.3 billion and
Rs. 24.6 billion. This is no longer merely about children needing spectacles.
Early-onset, progressive myopia raises the lifetime risk of retinal
complications, glaucoma and myopic maculopathy. Reduced outdoor activity,
intensive near-work and prolonged screen use, greatly worsened by the shift to
online schooling during the pandemic are established contributors. Children
from weaker sections often remain undiagnosed, and uncorrected vision quietly
damages their learning.
I therefore urge the Government to institute a
National Childhood Myopia Prevention and Control Programme providing for annual
vision screening of schoolchildren; integration with the School Health and
Wellness Programme and Ayushman Bharat; national clinical guidelines on outdoor
activity, near-work and device use; myopia clinics in government hospitals and
medical colleges; affordable spectacles and myopia-control measures for poor
children; national surveillance and research; and a sustained public-awareness
campaign for parents and teachers. Childhood is the critical period of ocular
development; preventive action now will avert avoidable blindness tomorrow.
(ENDS)
